**A Physician's Counsel**

A physician of eminence, some years ago,
Was summoned to attend a lady of fashion,
Who had long been admired — the toast of each beau,
Though now her sunken features excited compassion.

No sooner had the doctor the lady espied,
Than he begged she would, for once, his freedom forgive,
Should he step from the rules of good breeding aside,
To mention the terms upon which she might live.

"By all means," cried the lady, "for surely no word
A physician may utter should ever give offence;
Punctilio, in illness, is always absurd,
And betrays in the doctor or patient a want of sense."

"Why then, my dear lady, I cannot resist
Pronouncing this truth, like a plain, honest man:
That if in the use of white paint you persist,
No medicine can save you, do all that I can."

"You astonish me, Doctor! Yet such is my case,
That I may as well perish as leave paint alone;
For should I appear with my natural face
Amongst my acquaintance — I never should be known."

---

I have preserved the poem's original meaning, characters, and narrative while gently refining word choices ("summoned" for "called in," "espied" for "eyed," "betrays" for "shows," "perish" for "die") and smoothing the metre for a more elegant, professional cadence. Should you prefer a version that departs further from the original phrasing, I would be happy to provide one.
outputs.L2:
Many years back, a distinguished doctor was summoned to care for a fashionable woman. She had once been widely admired and celebrated by every gentleman suitor, but her wasted appearance now inspired only pity.

The moment the doctor examined her, he asked her to pardon his boldness just this once, if he set aside proper etiquette to explain the conditions under which she might survive.

"Please, go ahead," the lady replied. "Certainly nothing a doctor says could ever be offensive. Being overly formal during sickness is ridiculous and reveals that either the physician or the patient lacks good judgment."

"Very well then, my dear lady, I must speak this truth as an honest and straightforward man: if you continue using white face paint, no treatment I provide will be able to rescue you."

"I'm shocked, Doctor! Yet my situation is such that I might as well perish as abandon my cosmetics. After all, if I showed my bare face among the people I know, they wouldn't even recognize me."
outputs.L3:
# The Vanity of Appearances

A prominent physician of considerable reputation was once summoned to attend a lady who had, in her younger years, been celebrated throughout society for her remarkable beauty. Now, however, that beauty had faded, and the condition in which he found her was one that aroused not admiration but pity. Time and illness had worked their changes upon her, and it was clear to the experienced doctor that her situation was grave.

Wishing to help her as best he could, the physician approached the matter with the seriousness it demanded. He asked the lady's permission to speak frankly, requesting that they set aside the usual courtesies and polite formalities of social conversation. Only by speaking plainly, he explained, could he properly discuss what she must do if she wished to survive her affliction.

The lady, to her credit, agreed to this at once. She declared that standing upon ceremony during a time of genuine illness was the height of foolishness, and that such affectation reflected poorly upon doctor and patient alike. Let him speak his mind honestly, she urged, for she was prepared to hear whatever he had to say.

Encouraged by her willingness, the physician spoke bluntly. He warned her that no medicine, however potent, and no treatment, however skilled, could restore her health unless she first agreed to abandon one particular habit: she must cease applying the white paint and cosmetics with which she was accustomed to cover her face. These preparations, he made clear, were poisoning her, and no cure was possible while she continued to use them.

Yet here, at the very threshold of her recovery, the lady's resolve failed her entirely. For all her earlier good sense about setting aside vanity, she now refused outright to surrender her cosmetics. She would rather die, she insisted, than appear before the world with her natural, unadorned face. Without her paint, she protested, her acquaintances would no longer recognize her—and such a fate seemed to her worse than death itself.

# The Vanity of the Fashionable Lady

There lived in the city a physician whose reputation had spread through every quarter, so that the wealthy and the noble sought his counsel above all others. His judgment was esteemed as infallible, and his manner, though grave, was ever tempered with courtesy.

It happened that among his patients was a lady much admired in fashionable circles, celebrated for her beauty and the brilliance of her company. Of late, however, a sickness had come upon her, sapping the color from her cheeks and the strength from her limbs, so that those who loved her grew fearful for her life. The physician was summoned, and he attended her with all the care his art could furnish.

Having observed her condition through many days, he perceived at last the true source of her decline. Yet, knowing how delicate a matter it was, he first begged her leave to speak with perfect honesty.

"Madam," said he, "I must ask your permission to declare plainly what I have discovered, though the truth may not be welcome to your ear."

The lady, trusting in his wisdom, granted him leave.

"Then I must tell you," he continued, "that the white paint with which you daily adorn your face is a slow poison to your constitution. It has entered your blood and undermined your health. No remedy that I can offer, no treatment however diligent, will avail you so long as you persist in its use. You must abandon these cosmetics, or they will surely prove the death of you."

The lady heard him out, but far from being moved to gratitude or alarm, she received his warning with disdain.

"Sir," she replied, "I would sooner die than go without my paint. Were I to appear before the world in my natural complexion, not one of my acquaintances would know me. I should become a stranger to my own friends, and what is life to me if I am not myself in their eyes? Keep your cures, if the price of them is that I must be plain."

And so she dismissed the good physician, choosing the ornament of her face above the preservation of her life.

**The Moral:** How powerful a tyrant is vanity, that it can master even that instinct which nature has planted deepest in every living thing—the desire to preserve one's own life. The foolish will embrace their ruin rather than surrender the illusions upon which their pride is built.
outputs.L5:
# Questions That Shape Us

Sometimes the smallest words carry the heaviest weight. Consider three simple ones: *was*, *who*, and *tho* (though). Each opens a door to reflection, memory, and possibility.

**Who** we are is a question that follows us throughout our lives. It isn't answered once and settled forever. Instead, it evolves with every choice we make, every relationship we build, and every challenge we overcome. Asking "who am I?" isn't a sign of confusion—it's the beginning of genuine self-discovery.

**Was** speaks to everything that came before. It is the language of memory, of history, of the version of ourselves we used to be. What *was* cannot be changed, but it can be understood. The past holds lessons that shape our present, reminding us how far we've traveled and how much we've grown. Reflecting on what *was* gives context to what is and what might yet be.

And then there is *tho*—**though**—the word of contradiction and hope. It acknowledges difficulty while refusing to surrender to it. "Though the road was hard, I kept going." "Though I didn't know who I would become, I moved forward anyway." *Though* is the bridge between struggle and resilience, the quiet insistence that hardship isn't the whole story.

Together, these three words form a kind of map: understanding what *was*, discovering *who* we are, and pressing on *though* the way is uncertain. In their simplicity lies a profound truth about being human—we are shaped by our past, defined by our questions, and driven by our determination to continue.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous 18th-century-style poem about a vain lady of fashion who visits a doctor, only to refuse his advice to stop using white lead face paint.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Lady and Her Leaden Cure**

Lady Fripperton, a nymph of high renown,
The fairest (so she swore) in all the town,
Whose cheek was whiter than the driven snow—
By art, not nature, made resplendent so—
Did feel one morn a most peculiar ache,
And bid her chairmen to the doctor take.

"Good sir," quoth she, "my head is fit to split,
My hands do tremble and my stomach's flit,
My teeth grow loose, my gums a ghastly grey,
And all my bloom seems creeping fast away!"
The doctor peered, and stroked his learned chin,
And marked the ashen pallor of her skin.

"Madam," he sighed, "the cause is plain to see:
'Tis in that ceruse paint you daub so free.
The lead, dear lady, poisons vein and breath—
Each morning's toilet courts a slow, sure death.
Wash off this white! Let Nature take her seat,
Or soon you'll grace a churchyard's cold conceit."

The lady blanched—then blushed beneath her white,
And drew herself up rigid with affright.
"Wash off my face?! You quack, you dolt, you goose!
Go bleed the vulgar, but respect my ceruse!
What's health," she cried, "to one of my degree,
When all the beau monde marvels so at me?

"Shall Lady Bumford flaunt a brighter brow
While I, complexionless, disgrace my vow?
I'd sooner perish porcelain and grand
Than live one hour with freckles on my hand!
Keep, sir, your physic, sermons, and your fears—
I'll be the whitest corpse upon my bier!"

With that she flounced, and swept out through the door,
And left the doctor gaping on the floor.
Three months she reigned, the palest of the fair—
Then paler still, they laid her out with care.
And o'er her tomb this epitaph was read:
*Here lies a lady, faithful to her lead.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical narrative poem in rhyming quatrains about the dangers of cosmetic vanity, set among high society.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Countess and the Alchemist

In Belgravia lived the Countess Vane,
Whose mirror was her dearest, closest friend;
She studied every pore with fierce disdain
And swore each wrinkle was a foe to end.

At thirty-nine she wept before the glass,
"Alas! A crow has walked upon my eye!"
While suitors, poets, all the gilded class
Still praised her beauty—yet she wondered why.

"They flatter me because I am a Vane,
But truth resides in silvered looking-glass;
It never lies, it whispers cold and plain:
Your bloom, dear girl, is very apt to pass."

So off she went to Dr. Malachai,
An alchemist of dubious repute,
Who promised youth for those who dared to buy
And kept his ledgers thick with gold and loot.

"My cream," he purred, "contains the rarest things:
The dew of dawn, the tears of virgin swans,
Some powdered pearl, the dust from angels' wings,
And essence brewed beneath auspicious dawns."

(The truth, of course, was arsenic and lead,
With mercury to give the skin its glow;
A dash of belladonna, so 'tis said,
To make the pupils large and eyes to grow.)

She bathed in it. She drank it down like wine.
She painted thick her cheeks and swanlike throat.
"At last," she cried, "the years I shall decline!
I'll be the fairest face of note!"

And true, at first, a curious pallor came—
A marble whiteness, ghostly and refined.
The ton declared her beauty quite aflame;
The Duchess Frost was positively pined.

They flocked to learn her secret, one and all,
The ladies of the season, prim and proud,
And soon the fashionable had a ball
Devoted to the poison they'd allowed.

Lady Fitzhugh grew luminous and pale;
Miss Ashby's teeth went black but oh, so chic!
The Dowager, though somewhat green and frail,
Insisted she had never felt so sleek.

But mercury, that patient little sprite,
Was busy with his slow and certain art:
He loosened teeth by day and mind by night
And nibbled gently at each vital part.

The Countess trembled now when raising tea;
Her lovely hands would shudder, spill, and shake.
"How delicate!" the courtiers agreed,
"How fashionably fragile, for her sake!"

Her hair began to thin, then fall in clumps.
"A wig!" cried Malachai. "The latest rage!"
Her skin, once smooth, erupted into lumps
That powder hid—the powder of the age.

Still on she went, and deeper spread the rot,
For beauty is a debt one always pays;
She could not stop, she would not, dared not, not
While mirrors ruled the measure of her days.

One glittering night at Lady Carew's fête,
Beneath ten thousand candles' amber shine,
The Countess Vane, resplendent, met her fate
Mid crystal, silk, and rivers of champagne wine.

She rose to dance a stately, sweeping turn,
Her painted smile a masterpiece of white—
Then paused, as though she'd something grave to learn,
And crumpled, like a candle, into night.

The doctors came. They shook their heads and sighed.
"Some fever of the blood," they gravely said.
No soul suspected beauty's cream had lied,
Or that her vanity had struck her dead.

They buried her in Kensington in June,
Still powdered, rouged, and lovely in her bier;
The mourners wept beneath a cloudless moon
And called her "fairest flower of the year."

And Dr. Malachai? He prospered on,
For grief and fashion never lose their grip;
Before the Countess Vane was fully gone,
A hundred ladies queued to buy his script.

So heed the tale of her who could not bear
To let a single season leave its trace—
Who traded life and sense for looking fair,
And met her Maker with a lovely face.

The moral, friends, is neither deep nor odd:
That beauty bought is beauty best refused;
The glass will flatter, but it plays at God,
And vainest hearts are soonest cruelly used.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a witty dialogue poem between a physician and a fashionable lady who would rather die than give up her makeup?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Physician and the Fashionable Lady**

*The Doctor:*
"Madam, I fear I must be blunt—
Your health has borne a dreadful brunt.
That lead-white powder on your face
Is hurrying you toward the grave."

*The Lady:*
"Oh Doctor, spare me your report,
My complexion is my last resort.
A pallor pure as winter's frost
Is worth whatever health it cost."

*The Doctor:*
"But look! Your gums have taken flight,
Your teeth are loosening left and right,
Your hands do tremble, cheeks grow thin—
The poison seeps beneath your skin."

*The Lady:*
"A trembling hand is quite the rage,
It's fashionable in this age.
And should my teeth abandon me,
I'll smile with cool serenity."

*The Doctor:*
"That rouge you wear of vermilion red
Contains the mercury I dread.
Each morning's paint, each evening's cream,
Shall stop your heart—or so I deem."

*The Lady:*
"Then let it stop, but stop it grand!
I'll die the belle of all the land.
What use is breath, what use is pulse,
If one must look a country dolt?"

*The Doctor:*
"I've cured the pox, I've set the bone,
But never met a will of stone.
You'd trade your years, your very life—"

*The Lady:*
"For beauty, sir? Without a knife!
Now off you go with all your fuss—
I've powder yet, and much to truss.
Death may arrive with dreary tread,
But he shall find me *well* in red."

*The Doctor:* *(departing)*
"Then vanity shall write your end.
Good day, dear madam."

*The Lady:*
"...Farewell, my friend.
And should I meet Saint Peter's stare,
I'll ask him kindly—*do I glare?*"
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**On the Vanity of Painted Cheeks**

*Inscribed to the Ladies of Fashion*

Ye tender fair, who court the glass's praise,
And on your cheeks the borrow'd lily raise,
Attend the Muse, who mourns your ruin'd bloom,
And reads your beauty's warrant to the tomb.

That snowy white, which artful hands prepare,
Is Death's own livery, though it seem so fair;
The ceruse creeps where healthful roses grew,
And drinks the crimson from your natural hue.

Fond nymph! that paint which decks thy morning face
By night hath stol'n the substance for the grace;
Each glist'ring layer that flatters to the eye
Doth teach thy teeth to loosen, cheek to die.

Where is the freshness Nature freely gave,
Ere Folly led it captive to the grave?
Thou paint'st a corpse, and call'st the labour Art,
And hid'st with lead the wreck of every part.

Go, ask the beldam whom thy mirrors flee—
Once such a bloom as now beguileth thee;
Her hollow'd temples, and her sallow skin,
Proclaim the poison she took pride to win.

Learn, then, sweet maid, ere yet the harm be sped:
True bloom springs inward, not from paint of lead;
A cheerful heart, a conscience clean and light,
Shall keep thee fairer than that fatal white.

So shall thy beauty, temperate and true,
Outlast the season's transitory hue;
While she who trusts the pot her charms to save
Shall find her looking-glass become her grave.

---

*If you'd like, I can adjust the meter, extend it, or lean harder toward a particular era (Georgian broadsheet vs. Victorian temperance-tract style).*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a comic poem where a plain-spoken doctor warns an aging society beauty about her face paint, and she comically prefers death to being unrecognizable.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Consultation of Lady Vermilion**

The doctor, a man of no delicate phrase,
Was summoned to physic a face full of glaze.
He entered the boudoir, and gave a great start—
For there sat the Beauty, a masterwork's art:

Two inches of powder, a rouge like a rose,
A ceruse so thick it near buried her nose,
Some varnish, some lacquer, a lead-tinted paste,
And beauty-spots dotted about with great taste.

"Good madam," said he, in his plain country way,
"I've come, as you begged, for I heard you're not gay.
Your color's alarming, your breathing is weak—
And frankly, dear lady, there's *rot* on your cheek.

"That white that you wear is the poison called lead;
It's eating your visage and clouding your head.
Wash off all that plaster, that varnish, that lard,
Or physic won't help you—you'll die in the yard."

The Beauty grew pale (though one could not quite tell),
And gripped at her bosom, and let out a knell:
"You brute! You barbarian! You physicking clod!
Would you have me stand naked and bald before God?

"Beneath all this splendor—O horror! O shame!—
There lurks an old woman that *no one* could name!
My friends would not know me! My lovers would flee!
The mirror itself would deny it was me!

"I'd rather be buried in powder and paint,
A gorgeous cadaver, a well-lacquered saint,
Than live one dull hour with a countenance bare—
So *keep* your foul cure, sir, and mind your own hair!"

The doctor bowed low, took his fee, and withdrew,
Remarking, "Well, madam, the choice is with you.
Some fear the cold grave, and some dread the disease—
But you, ma'am, fear *washing* far greater than these."

So she perished, in time, in her armor of white,
A monument grand to society's plight;
And carved on her tomb, where the ivy now creeps:
*She saved her complexion. It's here that it sleeps.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
